582.title: Four kinds of samana
582.hook: Cunda the smith asks how many kinds of wandering seekers there are
582.howItsDone: Buddhist communities have long relied on the monastic code and on lay supporters to tell sincere practitioners from impostors, and teachers often cite Cunda's poem when misconduct comes to light.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Buddha's farm, and your line, faith the seed. Did you plant something small? Today a craftsman asks a sharp question about the people who wear the robe. Day five hundred eighty-two.

A news story breaks about a religious leader somewhere who did something terrible. And at the dinner table, someone says: see, they're all the same. Every tradition hears that sentence sooner or later. The fifth poem of the Sutta Nipata takes it on directly. A metalworker named Cunda, the smith's son, asks the Buddha a practical question. How many kinds of samanas are there in the world? Samana means a wandering seeker, someone who has left home for the spiritual life. Cunda wants to know how to tell them apart. Today: four kinds of samana.
screen: `THEY'RE ALL THE SAME.` → `CUNDA THE SMITH ASKS.` → `HOW DO YOU TELL THEM APART?`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers: there are four, and no fifth. The first is the one who has conquered the path: beyond doubt, free of the arrow, delighting in freedom, a guide for the world. The second is the one who shows the path: someone who knows the highest as the highest, and explains it and lays it out right here, cutting through other people's doubts. The third is the one who lives the path: well restrained, mindful, walking the well-taught way, doing no harm. And the fourth is the one who defiles the path. He wears the same robe as the good ones. He looks the part. But he's pushy, deceitful, unrestrained, a fraud in disguise, and he spoils the families who trust him. The poem calls him chaff. Then comes the line that answers the dinner table. A lay follower who has heard and understood this, the poem says, sees the fourth kind for what he is, and doesn't lose trust in the others because of him. How could the pure and the impure be the same? Notice the order. The Buddha himself is usually understood as the first. But the second, the one who shows, is any good teacher who explains clearly and clears up doubt. You don't have to have arrived to point the way well. And the warning in the fourth is honest: the robe alone proves nothing. A tradition that names its own frauds, plainly, in one of its oldest poems, is taking trust seriously.
screen: `THE ONE WHO HAS CONQUERED THE PATH` · `THE ONE WHO SHOWS IT, THE ONE WHO LIVES IT` · `THE ONE WHO DEFILES IT` · `ONE FRAUD DOESN'T MAKE THEM ALL` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO SHOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who showed you a good path. Sit and settle. A teacher, a coach, a grandparent, a friend who explained something kindly. Not someone who had it all figured out; someone who pointed clearly. See their face. Thank them silently. Then ask: is there a small path I could show someone today? A shortcut at work, a recipe, a calmer way to handle a hard thing. Let one name come. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Four kinds of samana. Cunda's question: the one who conquers the path, the one who shows it, the one who lives it, and the one who wears the robe and defiles it. Today's word.
Your line: the one who shows. Show someone one good path today, clearly and kindly, without needing to be the expert. Day five hundred eighty-two.

options: stop trusting every monk.

original.note: Pali samana (Sanskrit shramana): a wandering seeker who has left home, of any school in the Buddha's India.

trapdoor: what you thought: a samana is a Buddhist monk.
what it means: a samana is any wandering seeker who has left home; Cunda's poem sorts them into four kinds.

what a scholar hears: the Pali names are roughly maggajina, maggadesaka (or maggakkhayi), magge jivati and maggadusi; the shramana movements included Jains, Ajivikas and others alongside the Buddha's followers.

583.title: Downfall
583.hook: a shining visitor asks, again and again: and what is the next cause of downfall?
583.howItsDone: The Parabhava Sutta is among the protective discourses chanted in Theravada communities, and it is often taught to lay Buddhists as practical advice on family, money and friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Cunda's four kinds of seeker, and your line, the one who shows. Did you show someone a good path? Today, the opposite direction: how people slide. Day five hundred eighty-three.

Nobody wakes up one morning and decides to wreck their life. It goes slower than that. A habit here, a skipped call to a parent there, a little more money spent than earned, a little more pride than the situation needed. Years later, it adds up. The sixth poem of the Sutta Nipata is a slow-motion map of that slide. Late at night, a shining deity lights up the grove where the Buddha is staying and asks one question, then keeps coming back with the same follow-up: that's one. Tell me the next. Today: downfall.
screen: `NOBODY DECIDES TO FALL.` → `A SHINING VISITOR AT NIGHT.` → `TELL ME THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Parabhava Sutta, the discourse on downfall, or decline. It opens simply: the one who rises is easy to know, and the one who falls is easy to know. Whoever loves the good teaching rises; whoever hates it falls. Then the visitor asks for the next cause, and the next, about a dozen in all. Some of them sound ancient, addressed to a man of that time. But listen to how many land today. Keeping company with bad people and liking their ways. Loving sleep, loving crowds, never making an effort, quick to anger. Being able to support your aging mother and father, and not doing it. Lying to a holy person to deceive them. Having plenty of wealth and good food, and eating it alone. Being proud of your family, your money or your name, and looking down on your own relatives. Drinking, gambling, chasing affairs, and losing what you earn. Putting a reckless spender in charge of your affairs. Having little and wanting a throne. Notice what's barely on the list: ritual. Apart from the first verse, about the teaching itself, and a few on sloth and appetite, the causes are ways of treating people: parents, relatives, the hungry, the trusting. Downfall here is mostly relational. And notice one quiet detail: the wealthy person isn't condemned for being wealthy, only for eating alone. The poem closes by saying the wise, seeing these causes of downfall clearly, take the safe road.
screen: `THE ONE WHO RISES IS EASY TO KNOW` · `TELL ME THE NEXT CAUSE` · `PARENTS, RELATIVES, THE HUNGRY` · `NOT RICH: RICH AND EATING ALONE` · then, large: `CAUSES OF DOWNFALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one downfall to avoid today. Sit and settle. Go through the list quietly: bad company, too much sleep, a parent who needs a call, a meal not shared, pride in front of family, money leaking away. Which one is closest to your life right now? Don't judge yourself. Just pick it. Then picture one small move away from it: a call, a shared plate, an early night. Hold that picture for a few breaths, then rest. The bell holds the time.
Downfall. The Parabhava Sutta: about a dozen ways a person slowly falls, almost all of them about how we treat the people around us. Today's word.
Your line: causes of downfall. Take your one small move away from the one you picked, before the day ends. Day five hundred eighty-three.

original.note: Pali parabhava: decline, downfall, ruin. the name of Sn 1.6.

trapdoor: what you thought: downfall means one dramatic mistake.
what it means: in the poem it's a slow slide through small causes, almost all about how we treat others.
what a scholar hears: the Parabhava Sutta is paired in tradition with the Mangala Sutta, decline and blessing, and both are chanted as protective discourses.

584.title: By deeds
584.hook: a man shouts 'outcast!' at the Buddha, and gets a question back
584.howItsDone: The Vasala Sutta is chanted as one of the protective discourses in Theravada communities, and its line 'not by birth, by deeds' is widely quoted by Buddhists speaking about dignity and caste.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the slow slide, and your line, causes of downfall. Did you make your one small move? Today, an insult shouted across a doorway, and a calm reply. Day five hundred eighty-four.

Morning in the city of Savatthi. In one house a brahmin named Aggika Bharadvaja has his sacred fire burning and his offerings laid out, everything ready and pure. And walking down the street with his alms bowl comes the Buddha. To this man, at this moment, a shaven-headed wanderer near his fire is a kind of pollution. So he shouts. Stop there, shaveling! Stop there, you wretched monk! Stop there, outcast! Most of us know what we'd do next. Shout back, or walk away hurt. The Buddha does neither. Today: by deeds.
screen: `A SACRED FIRE, READY AND PURE.` → `STOP THERE, OUTCAST!` → `NEITHER SHOUTING NOR LEAVING.`

segments.voice: He asks a question. Do you know, brahmin, what an outcast is, or what makes someone one? And the brahmin, maybe surprised, says: no, I don't. Teach me. So the Buddha does, in verse. In his society the word for outcast, vasala, named people by birth: the families whose very presence was thought to stain. The Buddha keeps the word and changes what earns it. Whoever is angry and holds grudges, he says, is an outcast. Whoever harms living beings. Whoever steals, or borrows money and then denies the debt. Whoever lies as a witness. Whoever is able to support aging parents and doesn't. Whoever strikes or insults their family. Whoever does wrong and hopes no one will find out. Whoever praises themselves and looks down on others. Then he tells of Matanga, a man born into the most despised group of all, who became so honored that nobles and brahmins came to serve him. His birth didn't stop him. And then the line: not by birth is one an outcast, not by birth is one a brahmin. By deeds one becomes an outcast; by deeds one becomes a brahmin. Here's what's easy to miss. The list of outcast deeds is long, and the man who just shouted is standing right there, angry, looking down on someone. The Buddha never says so. He just describes it, and lets the brahmin find himself in it. At the end, the brahmin asks to become a follower.
screen: `DO YOU KNOW WHAT AN OUTCAST IS?` · `ANGRY, CRUEL, LOOKING DOWN ON OTHERS` · `MATANGA, BORN LOW, HONORED HIGH` · `NOT BY BIRTH: BY DEEDS` · then, large: `BY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat one person as noble today, and begin in the mind now. Sit and settle. Think of someone people tend to overlook or look down on: the person who empties the bins, the new kid, the neighbor nobody greets. See them clearly. Notice one good deed you've seen them do, or could imagine them doing. Let that deed, not their place, be what you see. Then decide on one small way to treat them with honor today. A name, a thank-you, eye contact. The bell holds the time.
By deeds. The Buddha's answer to the brahmin who called him an outcast: no one is low or noble by birth, only by what they do. Today's word.
Your line: by deeds. When you catch yourself sizing someone up by where they come from today, swap the question: what do they do? Day five hundred eighty-four.

original.note: Pali kammuna: by action, by deeds (from kamma). the key word in 'by deeds one becomes an outcast'.

trapdoor: what you thought: an outcast is someone born into the lowest group.
what it means: in this poem an outcast is anyone who is cruel, dishonest or contemptuous, whatever their birth.

what a scholar hears: the Buddha reuses the brahmin's own vocabulary, vasala and brahmana, and redefines both by conduct; the same line returns in the Vasettha Sutta and the Dhammapada's last chapter.

585.title: Kindness, read again
585.hook: the loving-kindness discourse, read whole, start to finish
585.carry: as a mother her only child
585.howItsDone: The Karaniya Metta Sutta is chanted in Pali daily in many Theravada temples and homes, often by heart, and is one of the most common protective chants.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the man who shouted outcast, and your line, by deeds. Did you treat someone as noble? Today, a text you've met before, read the whole way through. Day five hundred eighty-five.

There's a song you've loved since you were a kid, and one day you hear the whole album version for the first time, with the verse they cut from the radio. Same song, and suddenly it's bigger. More than a year ago, in the first months of this path, we spent days on loving-kindness, metta, and on its most famous image. Now, reading the Sutta Nipata in order, we arrive at the poem itself, the eighth piece in the book. Ten short verses. Today we hear it start to finish, and notice the shape. Today's word: kindness.
screen: `THE ALBUM VERSION.` → `THE EIGHTH POEM IN THE BOOK.` → `START TO FINISH.`

segments.voice: The poem moves in three steps. First, how to live. Before any wishing, it describes a person: capable, upright, gentle, easy to speak to, not proud, content, not weighed down by busyness, calm in the senses, not greedy with families. Doing nothing the wise would criticize. Kindness starts as a way of behaving. Second, the wishes. May all beings be happy and at ease. Weak or strong, long or short, big or small, seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born: may all beings be happy. Let no one deceive another or look down on anyone anywhere, or wish harm on anyone in anger. And then the image at the center: just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let one cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. Notice it's the boundlessness being compared: a love that doesn't measure. Third, the reach. Kindness spreading above, below and all around, without obstruction, without hatred, without enmity. Standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as you're awake, keep this mindfulness. This, the poem says, is called a divine way of living, right here. And the last verse surprises people. It doesn't end on love. It ends on seeing: not grasping at views, having clear vision, letting go of greed for sense pleasures, such a one won't be born again into a womb. Kindness, in this poem, isn't only warm. It's a path to waking up.
screen: `FIRST, HOW TO LIVE` · `THEN THE WISHES: ALL BEINGS` · `A MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD` · `ABOVE, BELOW, ALL AROUND` · then, large: `AS A MOTHER HER ONLY CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite it, in your own way. Sit and settle. Say the wishes slowly, in the poem's order. May all beings be happy and at ease. The weak and the strong. The seen and the unseen. Those near and those far. Those born, and those yet to be born. Then picture the mother bent over her only child, and let that same unmeasured care spread out: above you, below you, all around. If you know the Pali, you can chant it instead. Then rest inside that wide feeling. The bell holds the time.
Kindness. Metta, as the poem lays it out whole: a way of living, a set of wishes for all beings, and a boundless heart spreading in every direction. Today's word.
Your line: as a mother her only child. Today, when you're standing, walking or sitting somewhere ordinary, send the poem's wish to everyone in sight. Day five hundred eighty-five.

fork.reveal: a mother and her only child: the comparison is to love without measure, spread to every being.

original.note: Pali metta (Sanskrit maitri): loving-kindness, friendliness, from mitta, friend.

trapdoor: what you thought: the metta sutta is a sweet poem about feeling love for everyone.
what it means: it moves from conduct, to wishes for all beings, to kindness filling every direction, and ends on clear seeing.

what a scholar hears: the mother verse can be read as comparing the boundlessness of the heart rather than literal protection; the poem appears in both the Sutta Nipata (1.8) and the Khuddakapatha (9).

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta (also Khuddakapatha 9)

586.title: Two spirits talk
586.hook: two mountain spirits check the Buddha's character before they go to meet him
586.howItsDone: Buddhist texts encourage people to examine a teacher's conduct and speech over time before placing trust in them, and the full-moon uposatha days are still when many lay Buddhists visit temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the kindness poem, whole, and your line, as a mother her only child. Did you send the wish to a room full of strangers? Today, two spirits on a mountain, gossiping. Day five hundred eighty-six.

Before you hire someone, you call their references. Before you try a new doctor, you ask a friend: is she any good? Not her diploma. Her. Does she listen? Is she honest? The ninth poem of the Sutta Nipata is a reference check, done by two yakkhas, nature spirits of the hills. It's a full-moon night, the holy day. One spirit, Satagira, says to his friend: tonight's a special night. Let's go see the teacher Gotama. And his friend Hemavata, from the Himalaya, says: wait. First, tell me about him. Today: two spirits talk.
screen: `CALL THE REFERENCES.` → `A FULL MOON ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `WAIT. TELL ME ABOUT HIM.`

segments.voice: Hemavata's questions come in a steady rhythm, and Satagira answers every one. Is his mind well disposed toward all beings? It is. Does he master his reactions to what he likes and what he doesn't? He does. Does he take what isn't given? He doesn't. Is he restrained toward living things, never careless, never neglecting meditation? He is. Does he lie? Speak harshly? Carry tales between people? Chatter about nothing? No, no, no and no. His words, Satagira says, are measured and full of sense. Is he free from craving, his mind clear, does he have the eye that sees the truth? Yes. Notice what Hemavata doesn't ask. Not: can he do miracles? Not: how famous is he? Not even: what does he teach? Every question is about character. How he treats beings. How he speaks. Whether his mind is steady. That's the test the poem sets for a teacher. And notice Satagira. He doesn't exaggerate or sell. He simply answers, honestly, one question at a time, and in doing it he speaks well of someone good. Then the two spirits go down the mountain and ask the Buddha their own questions. What does the world arise in? In six, he says: the six senses. At the end, the poem says, the spirits decide to travel from village to village and mountain to mountain, honoring the Buddha and the teaching. A good reputation, carried by a friend's honest words, became a journey.
screen: `WAIT: TELL ME ABOUT HIM FIRST` · `HOW HE TREATS BEINGS, HOW HE SPEAKS` · `CHARACTER, NOT MIRACLES` · `AN HONEST FRIEND'S GOOD WORD` · then, large: `THEY SPOKE WELL OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak well of someone good, starting in your head. Sit and settle. Choose someone you respect: a teacher, a coworker, a relative. Ask Hemavata's questions about them, quietly. Are they kind to people? Do they tell the truth? Do they avoid gossip? Let honest answers come, not flattery. Notice which answers make you glad. Then pick one true, specific good thing about them that you could say out loud to someone else today. Hold it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Two spirits talk. Hemavata asks about the Buddha's character, Satagira answers honestly, and a good word, well spoken, sends them down the mountain. Today's word.
Your line: they spoke well of him. Say your one true good thing about that person to someone else today, when they're not in the room. Day five hundred eighty-six.

fork.reveal: Hemavata's questions are all about character: kindness to beings, honest speech, a steady mind.

original.note: Pali yakkha (Sanskrit yaksha): a nature spirit of trees, hills or wild places, sometimes kind, sometimes fierce.

trapdoor: what you thought: two spirits talking is a fairy tale.
what it means: it's a reference check: one friend asks about a teacher's character, the other answers honestly.
what a scholar hears: the Hemavata Sutta's questions echo the list of the Buddha's virtues in the Long Discourses, and yakkhas appear across early texts as local spirits who become followers.

587.title: Faith the best wealth
587.hook: a fierce spirit orders the Buddha in and out, then threatens him with a riddle
587.howItsDone: The taming of Alavaka is one of the episodes recalled in the Jayamangala Gatha, a verse chant of the Buddha's victories recited in many Theravada temples and homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two mountain spirits checking references, and your line, they spoke well of him. Did you say your good word? Today, a much less friendly spirit. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

Get out. So the Buddha gets up and goes out. Come in. So he comes back in. Get out. He goes. Come in. He comes. The spirit is a yakkha named Alavaka, and this is his house, and he's testing how far he can push this calm visitor. The fourth time he says get out, the Buddha says: no, friend, I won't. Do what you have to do. And Alavaka makes his threat. I'll ask you a question. If you can't answer it, I'll scramble your mind, or split your heart, or grab you by the feet and throw you across the Ganges. Today: faith the best wealth.
screen: `GET OUT. COME IN.` → `THE FOURTH TIME: NO.` → `ANSWER, OR ELSE.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's reply is calm. In all the world, he says, I see no one who could scramble my mind or split my heart. But ask whatever you like. Notice the order of what he did. Three times, he went along. Not because he was afraid, the commentary says, but to soften a hard mind with gentleness. Only the fourth time, when obeying would have been just a game, did he say no. Then the questions come, in verse. What is the best wealth a person has? Faith, the Buddha answers, saddha, trust in what is good. What, practiced well, brings happiness? The teaching. What is the sweetest of all tastes? Truth. Living how is the best life? Living with wisdom. Then the deeper ones. How does one cross the flood? By faith. How does one cross the sea? By care, by not being careless. How does one get past suffering? By effort. How does one become pure? By wisdom. Why is faith the best wealth? Think about what the threat was. Alavaka could take everything: your mind, your body, your life. But trust in something good is a kind of wealth that's still yours while you're being threatened. It's what lets you answer calmly. And at the end, the fierce spirit says he'll travel from village to village, honoring the one who is fully awake. The taming of Alavaka is still recalled in chants in many Theravada temples.
screen: `THREE TIMES YES, THE FOURTH TIME NO` · `NO ONE CAN SPLIT MY HEART` · `THE BEST WEALTH IS FAITH` · `CROSS THE FLOOD BY TRUST` · then, large: `FAITH THE BEST WEALTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse one calm answer. Sit and settle. Think of a small threat you face: a demanding message, a tense meeting, a sharp relative. Picture it arriving. Feel the jolt in the chest. Now breathe out slowly, and picture yourself answering the way the Buddha did: not shrinking, not striking back. Just steady. Ask what it is they want, and answer plainly. Let your shoulders drop. Feel the wealth that's still yours. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Faith the best wealth. The Buddha's first answer to the threatening spirit Alavaka: trust in what is good is the wealth no threat can take. Today's word.
Your line: faith the best wealth. When something pushes you today, answer once from that steady place, calmly and plainly. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

screen: `DAY 587 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BODY AS IT IS.`

original.note: Pali Alavaka: the spirit of Alavi, named for the town where the story is set.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith as the best wealth means believing is better than having money.
what it means: trust in what is good is the one wealth a threat can't take, and it lets you answer calmly.
what a scholar hears: the Alavaka Sutta (Sn 1.10, also SN 10.12) pairs faith with crossing the flood; later tradition makes the taming of Alavaka one of the eight victories of the Jayamangala chant.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.10, Alavaka Sutta (also Samyutta Nikaya 10.12)

588.title: The body as it is
588.hook: walking, standing, sitting, lying down: a poem that looks at the body plainly
588.howItsDone: Contemplating the parts of the body is a traditional Buddhist meditation, taught especially to monastics; teachers present it as a way to loosen vanity and craving, not to cultivate disgust.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fierce spirit Alavaka, and your line, faith the best wealth. Did you answer one push calmly? Today ends the week, with the most ordinary thing you own. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

Some days you catch yourself in a shop window and think: not bad. Other days the bathroom mirror at seven in the morning says something else entirely. Most of us swing between those two, pride and dislike, about the same body, sometimes within the same hour. Phones add filters to fix one side; ads sell us the other. The eleventh poem of the Sutta Nipata asks for something rarer than either. Not a better body, not a worse opinion of it. Just a clear look. Today: the body as it is.
screen: `THE SHOP WINDOW: NOT BAD.` → `THE MIRROR AT 7 A.M.` → `SOMETHING RARER: A CLEAR LOOK.`

segments.voice: The poem starts with movement. Walking or standing, sitting or lying down, bending and stretching: that's what a body does. Then it looks inside, the way an honest anatomy lesson would. Bones and sinews, wrapped in skin and flesh. A belly, a liver, a heart, lungs, kidneys. Things the skin covers, so we don't see them as they are. Then it looks at what comes out: tears, sweat, the things that leave the body every day. Some listeners find this part uncomfortable, and that's worth noticing. The poem isn't trying to make anyone ashamed. Its last lines name the point. Whoever thinks highly of themselves because of a body like this, or looks down on someone else because of theirs, what is that, the poem asks, except not seeing? So the poem cuts in two directions at once. Against vanity: this body is not a trophy. And against contempt: no one is lesser because of theirs. What's left is something steady and kind: a body that walks and bends and breathes, seen plainly. This week has been about seeing plainly, too. Four kinds of seekers, and a robe that proves nothing. A slow slide, told cause by cause. Not by birth, by deeds. The kindness poem, whole. Two spirits checking character. A threat answered with calm. Each time, the poem looks past the surface, a robe, a birth, a threat, to what is actually there.

Somewhere inside, a heart is working, without asking for thanks. If a judgment comes, too heavy, too tired, not bad, just name it, judging, and come back to the plain feeling. Not good, not bad. Warm here, tight there, moving, breathing. A body, as it is, carrying you through another day. The bell holds the time.
